verdict_reason: The task computes what the manuscript defines (metrics_catalogue.tex:24 -- 'overall (strided sliding window, 1024-token context pinned across models), plus a rare/frequent-token decomposition and bits-per-byte'), and I reproduced the reference procedure head to head. Running BLME's strided_perplexity and the HuggingFace docs/source/en/perplexity.md snippet verbatim beside it on the FULL WikiText-2-raw test split (4,358 rows, window 1024 / stride 512, gpt2, one GPU on this host): BLME 25.17047937898196 against the HF snippet's 25.17040443420410, relative 2.98e-06 -- and the residue is entirely the HF snippet's own `num_loss_tokens = num_valid_tokens - input_ids.size(0)` quirk, which drops exactly one token per window (287,643 BLME vs 287,083 HF, difference 560 = the window count). BLME also matches HuggingFace's published figure for that page, 25.17041, to relative 2.8e-06. I REFUTE the round-5 codex RED on its verdict-driving item. Its claim is that the shared-offset EVEN SPLIT misattributes bytes at the scored/unscored boundary; the split is real (for GPT-2 `emoji`+`b` the exact byte ownership is [3,1,1] and BLME assigns [2,2,1], so 3 rather than 2 scored bytes, ratio 1.5000) but I measured its cost on the actual corpora and it is EXACTLY ZERO. I computed exact per-token byte ownership independently from GPT-2's byte-level token strings -- which sum to the corpus byte length exactly (1,296,370 = 1,296,370 on WikiText-2; 59,285 = 59,285 on the shipped default corpus) -- and compared the scored denominator: WikiText-2 exact 1,296,368 against BLME's reported 1,296,368 (difference 0 bytes, relative 0.000e+00), shipped corpus exact 59,281 against BLME's implied denominator 59,281.0000 (difference 0). The reason is structural, not luck: at the shipped stride = window/2 the ONLY unscored position in the whole stream is position 0, and 236 of 287,644 tokens share a span but none of them sits at that boundary. Codex's `emoji` case is a 5-byte, 3-token corpus, not the paper's domain.
comparable_reason: ppl_overall is tokenizer-dependent and therefore only loosely comparable across models with different vocabularies; bits_per_byte is the tokenizer-free member and is the right one for cross-model use, and its denominator is measurably exact (0 bytes off on 1,296,368). The genuine comparability caveat is a naming one: because the stream's first token is never scored, bits_per_byte is bits per SCORED byte, not bits per corpus byte -- 1,296,368 of 1,296,370 on WikiText-2 (a 1.5e-06 shortfall) and 59,281 of 59,285 on the shipped corpus. The second caveat is protocol, not comparability across models: ppl_rare / ppl_freq come from the PER-DOCUMENT pass while ppl_overall is the joined strided value, measured 37.908831 vs 21.804813 on gpt2 (1.738x), so a reader must not form ppl_rare/ppl_overall by hand. `_meta_ppl_bucket_protocol = per_document` discloses it and ppl_rare_over_freq = 5.280398 stays within one protocol. On the normalized variant itself: bits_per_byte normalizes away the TOKENIZER, and that mechanism is exact -- the denominator is the same corpus of source bytes for every model, and I verified it against independently computed exact per-token byte ownership at 0 bytes error on WikiText-2 (1,296,368) and on the shipped corpus (59,281). It does NOT remove a size association and is not meant to: this is a capability target, so YELLOW rather than GREEN on the campaign's normalized-twin bar, which asks for a measured reduction in an architectural association.
